title: Relativistic cosmology
one_line_summary: Builds the Robertson-Walker spacetime from the cosmological principle and Weyl's postulate, feeds a perfect fluid into Einstein's equations to get the Friedmann equations, and then derives cosmological redshift, a luminosity distance and the (approximate) Hubble law, after warming up with Olbers' paradox and a discrete Newtonian model.
role_in_book: Opens Part F (Cosmology) after the long treatment of black holes and gravitational radiation. It is the bridge from local exact solutions to a model of the whole universe: it assembles the symmetry assumptions and the kinematics (metric, redshift, distance, H and q) that Chapter 25 uses to classify and solve the classical Friedmann models and that Chapter 26 updates with multi-component LambdaCDM, CMB and inflation. It reuses tensor machinery from Chapter 6 (Weyl tensor in 3D), the perfect fluid and energy conditions of Chapter 12, the cosmological term and conservation laws of Chapter 13, and the spherically symmetric ansatz from Chapter 15.

assumed_background.topic: Riemann, Ricci and Einstein tensors; contracted Bianchi identities
Weyl tensor and its vanishing in three dimensions, eq. (6.88)
Ricci components of a general spherically symmetric line element (Exercise 6.32)
Perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor and energy conditions (12.64)
Field equations with cosmological term and conservation T^{ab}_{;b}=0
Isometries and Killing symmetries (group of isometries acting transitively)
Foliations of spacetime by spacelike hypersurfaces, hypersurface orthogonality
Null geodesics and proper time along timelike world-lines
Newtonian gravitational potential energy and conservation of energy for many-particle systems
Taylor expansion to second order; elementary integrals such as arcsin and arcsinh
Parametrizing spheres and hyperboloids; surface area and volume integrals in spherical coordinates
First law of thermodynamics dE + p dV = 0
Luminosity, flux, inverse-square law, apparent magnitude, galaxies and clusters

learning_objectives: State Olbers' paradox, reproduce the shell argument that a static, infinite, eternal, uniformly starry universe has a bright sky, and explain why finite age or expansion removes the paradox.

Build the discrete Newtonian cosmological model: impose radial scaling r_i(t)=S(t)r_i(t_0), derive Hubble's law v=Hr, and turn total energy conservation into an equation of the Friedmann form with k = +1, 0, -1.
State the cosmological principle and translate it into geometry: a foliation by spacelike slices that are homogeneous (transitive isometries) and isotropic about every point.
State Weyl's postulate and explain why it yields a perfect-fluid substratum, comoving coordinates and a cosmic time that is the proper time of fundamental observers.
Argue from similar triangles that time can enter the spatial metric only through an overall scale factor, g_{alpha beta}=S^2(t) h_{alpha beta}(x).
Show that isotropy about every point forces G^a_b proportional to the identity (an Einstein space), and that in three dimensions this means constant curvature.

Solve for the spherically symmetric 3-metric of constant curvature, obtain dr^2/(1-Kr^2)+r^2 d Omega^2, rescale to k=+1,0,-1, and write the Robertson-Walker line element in both the unbarred and conformally flat forms.

Describe the three spatial geometries: the 3-sphere embedded in Euclidean R^4 (finite volume 2 pi^2 R^3), flat R^3, and the hyperboloid embedded in Minkowski space (infinite volume), including how the area of geodesic spheres grows with radius in each.
Derive the two Friedmann equations for a perfect fluid with Lambda, recover energy conservation dE + p dV = 0 from them, and obtain the acceleration equation.
Use the acceleration equation and a tangent-line argument to prove the FRW singularity theorem and to bound the age of a decelerating universe by the Hubble time.
Integrate the dust case to Friedmann's equation Rdot^2 = C/R + Lambda R^2/3 - k and recognize it as identical to the Newtonian analogue.
Derive the cosmological redshift 1+z = R(t_0)/R(t_1) from two successive radial null rays, and distinguish it from a special-relativistic Doppler shift.

Distinguish absolute (proper) distance, angular-size distance and luminosity distance; explain the two factors of (1+z) in the flux, and derive z ~ H_0 d_L and the second-order correction involving q_0.
Define the deceleration parameter and relate q, H and rho through q = (4 pi rho/3 - Lambda/3)/H^2.

teaching_approach.summary: A classic Bondi-style introduction: the authors first make the reader feel why cosmology needs dynamics (Olbers' paradox) and how far Newtonian reasoning can go (a discrete model that already yields Hubble's law and a Friedmann-type energy equation). They then replace ad hoc Newtonian assumptions by carefully stated principles (cosmological principle, Weyl's postulate, general relativity) and derive, step by step, the metric, the dynamics and the observational relations. Geometry is made concrete through embeddings and by tracking how sphere areas grow with radius. The chapter ends by deducing, not assuming, Hubble's law, and calibrates the theory against rough observational numbers.
narrative_arc: Frame cosmology as modelling a unique system by smoothing out all structure; preview the hot big bang and caution that local physics is being extrapolated (§24.1).
Motivating puzzle: Olbers' shell argument shows a static infinite eternal universe would have a sky as bright as a stellar surface; resolutions point to youth or expansion (§24.2).

Newtonian warm-up: a finite set of galaxies moving radially with a common scale factor gives Hubble's law, and energy conservation (with a Lambda force) gives an equation of exactly the Friedmann form (§24.3).

Principles: state the cosmological principle, define homogeneity and isotropy precisely, review evidence (CMB), and survey alternatives (Bianchi, Kasner, hierarchical) before adopting it on pragmatic grounds (§24.4).
Weyl's postulate: galaxies as fluid particles on non-intersecting timelike geodesics give a unique velocity field, hence a perfect fluid (§24.5).
Kinematics: hypersurface orthogonality gives comoving coordinates and cosmic time; similar-triangle argument gives g=S^2(t)h(x); world map vs world picture (§24.6).
Geometry: isotropy everywhere implies Einstein space, which in 3D implies constant curvature; solve the spherically symmetric ansatz and rescale to Robertson-Walker form (§24.7).
Visualize k=+1,0,-1 via embedding in Euclidean or Minkowski 4-space, areas, volumes and topology (§24.8).

Dynamics: insert the perfect fluid into the field equations, obtain the two Friedmann equations, extract energy conservation, the acceleration equation and the FRW singularity theorem, then specialize to dust to get Friedmann's equation and note its identity with the Newtonian one (§24.9).
Observables: radial null geodesics give redshift 1+z=R_0/R_1 and a linear z-distance law for nearby sources (§24.10).
Distance: reject absolute and angular-size distances as impractical, define luminosity distance with two (1+z) factors, mention magnitudes and standard candles (§24.11).

Payoff: compute d_L=r_1 R_0 from homogeneity, deduce z~H_0 d_L, introduce Hubble time, deceleration parameter and its second-order effect, compare with Sandage's data, and link q to density and Lambda (§24.12).
signature_moves: Newtonian model first, then show the relativistic Friedmann equation is formally identical, while warning that the meaning of the terms differs.
Principles stated as highlighted postulates (cosmological principle, Weyl's postulate), each translated into a precise geometric condition.
Similar-triangles thought experiment to justify that the spatial metric only scales with time.
Eigenvector argument: isotropy leaves no preferred eigen-directions, so G^a_b must be a multiple of the identity.
Embedding diagrams of S^3 and the hyperboloid with one dimension suppressed, plus tracking the area of spheres versus radius to make curvature tangible.
Tangent-line (concavity) argument on the graph of R(t) to prove a finite-past big bang and bound the age by the Hubble time.
Successive-light-ray construction on a spacetime diagram to derive redshift without any velocity concept.
Physical bookkeeping of flux: photon arrival rate and photon energy each reduced by (1+z).
Explicit honesty about foundations: the cosmological principle is adopted because data are too sparse for anything weaker, not because it is proven.

sections.title: Preview
sections.summary: Defines cosmology as the dynamics of the universe treated as a smoothed-out whole, anticipates that symmetry reduces the dynamics to a first-order ODE (Friedmann's equation), and notes that Newtonian cosmology was constructed only after GR. Contrasts the perfect cosmological principle and steady state with the hot big bang, sketches the thermal history (radiation era, particle and element formation, then stars and galaxies), and stresses two epistemic caveats: local laws are extrapolated (Lambda is an example of a possible cosmic-scale interaction) and the universe is a unique, unrepeatable experiment.
key_moves: Smoothing assumption: ignore solar system, galaxy and cluster detail to capture only gross dynamics.
Newtonian and relativistic cosmology share the same starting simplicity principle.
Hot big bang timeline from radiation bath to galaxies; physics claimed reliable after about 1e-10 s (standard model) or 1e-43 s (GR plus GUTs).
No controlled repetition in cosmology: the system studied is unique.

sections.title: Olbers' paradox
sections.summary: Under Olbers' assumptions (Euclidean, infinite, static, eternal, uniform average stellar density and luminosity) every spherical shell contributes the same intensity, so the naive total diverges; including blocking by foreground stars caps it at the surface brightness of a star, still contradicting the dark sky. Thermodynamic equilibrium and line-of-sight arguments give the same conclusion. An absorbing gas does not help because it heats up and re-radiates, and curvature or finiteness of space does not change the conclusion. The resolution requires either a young universe (stars switched on recently) or expansion, whose redshift degrades distant light. The book notes a catch in the young-universe option: a short enough luminous history may conflict with the ages of the oldest stars.
key_moves: Shell of radius r, thickness dr: luminosity 4 pi r^2 dr l spread over area 4 pi r^2 gives l dr independent of r (24.1).
Sum of shells diverges; occultation by stars reduces it to stellar-surface brightness.
Equivalent arguments: equilibrium, every sightline ends on a star.
Half the radiation would come from beyond about 1e20 light years.
Absorbing gas refuted by thermal equilibrium; resolution by finite age or expansion.

sections.title: Newtonian cosmology
sections.summary: A finite system of n galaxies with pairwise Newtonian attraction plus a cosmological force F_i = Lambda m_i r_i/3. Spherical symmetry about an origin makes all motion radial, and preserving the pattern forces a universal scale factor S(t), so velocities obey Hubble's law v = H r with H = Sdot/S. Substituting into the conserved energy gives E = A Sdot^2 - B/S - D S^2 with positive constants; interpretation: with Lambda = 0 expansion must decelerate, positive Lambda repels, negative attracts. Rescaling S to R = mu S with mu^2 = A/|E| produces Rdot^2 = C/R + Lambda R^2/3 - k with k in {+1,0,-1}, the same form as the relativistic Friedmann equation, although the model only applies to a finite (arbitrarily large) universe.
key_moves: Radial motion from spherical symmetry (24.2).
Cosmological force and its potential energy (24.4)-(24.5).
Only uniform scaling is compatible with homogeneity: r_i(t)=S(t) r_i(t_0) (24.7).
Differentiate to get Hubble's law (24.10).
Energy equation (24.11) with A, B, D; note D = Lambda A/3.
Rescale by mu to normalize the energy constant into k = +1, 0, -1 (24.17)-(24.18).

sections.title: The cosmological principle
sections.summary: States the cosmological principle as a generalized Copernican principle and makes it precise: there is a cosmic time whose slices are homogeneous (an isometry group maps any point to any other) and isotropic about each point; global isotropy implies homogeneity. Homogeneity is meant only after averaging over cells larger than about 1e9 light years, bigger than superclusters (about 3e8 ly). Evidence: isotropy of radio galaxies, X-ray sources and quasars to better than 15%, supernova Hubble-constant measurements, and above all the CMB (2.7 K, isotropic to about 1 part in 1e5 per Planck); galaxy counts and a linear Hubble law support homogeneity. Surveys alternatives: Bianchi (homogeneous anisotropic) models, the vacuum Bianchi I Kasner metric with cigar and pancake singularities, whimper singularities, BKL, and Charlier's hierarchical model. The principle is adopted because weaker assumptions leave too many unknown functions for the available data.
key_moves: Formal definitions: homogeneity via transitive isometry group; isotropy as no preferred direction (spherical symmetry) about a point.
Global isotropy implies homogeneity.
Homogeneity holds only for a smeared-out universe averaged over >1e9 ly cells.
Three motivations for anisotropic/inhomogeneous models: galaxy formation, generic singularity structure (BKL), and washing-out mechanisms like inflation.
Kasner exponents satisfy sum p_i = sum p_i^2 = 1.
Pragmatic adoption: symmetric models are the only ones data can constrain.

sections.title: Weyl's postulate
sections.summary: Weyl (1923) confronted the tension between a generally covariant theory and a unique universe by singling out privileged observers who move with the smoothed galactic motion, justified by small local peculiar velocities. In Robertson's formulation, the world-lines of the substratum form a family of timelike geodesics that spread out from a single past point (finite or infinitely remote); since they do not cross (except at past/future singular points), each event has a unique fluid velocity and the substratum is a perfect fluid. Peculiar velocities below about 1e-3 c are neglected. The postulate is a useful starting point rather than a necessity.
key_moves: Uniqueness of the universe motivates a privileged class of observers.
Non-intersecting geodesic congruence gives a single velocity at each event.
Single velocity field justifies a perfect-fluid source.
Peculiar velocities (<1e-3 c) negligible compared with expansion velocities near c at large distances.

sections.title: Standard models of relativistic cosmology
sections.summary: The standard models rest on three assumptions: cosmological principle, Weyl's postulate, general relativity. Isotropy forces the substratum geodesics to be orthogonal to the slices (otherwise the tangent picks out a direction), giving comoving spatial coordinates constant along the geodesics and a cosmic time t with ds^2 = dt^2 - g_{alpha beta} dx^alpha dx^beta. Cosmic time defines simultaneity: the world map is the distribution of events on a slice, the world picture is what an observer sees on its past light cone. A small triangle of particles must evolve into a similar triangle with a position-independent magnification, so g_{alpha beta} = S^2(t) h_{alpha beta}(x); S must be real, and each slice must have constant curvature.
key_moves: Orthogonality of fluid world-lines to slices follows from isotropy.
Choose t so g_00 = 1 and g_0 alpha = 0.
Triangle-similarity argument forces separable time dependence (24.19).
Reality of S preserves the spacelike character of intervals.
Homogeneity and isotropy of slices requires constant curvature of h.

sections.title: Spaces of constant curvature
sections.summary: Defines a space of constant curvature by R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc). For any dimension, isotropy means the linear map G^a_b has no preferred eigenvectors, so G_ab = -K g_ab with K constant by the Bianchi identities, i.e. R_ab = 2K g_ab/(n-2): an Einstein space. In three dimensions the Weyl tensor vanishes, so Riemann is fixed by Ricci and an Einstein 3-space has constant curvature. Assuming spherical symmetry about a point, the Ricci equations for e^lambda dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 give e^{-lambda} = 1 - K r^2. An alternative radial coordinate gives a conformally flat form. Combining with §24.6 yields the cosmological line element; rescaling r and S absorbs |K| to leave k = +1, 0, -1 and the Robertson-Walker line element (24.36)/(24.37) and slice geometry (24.38).
key_moves: Isotropy => G^a_b proportional to delta^a_b.
Contracted Bianchi identity => K constant.
3D: substitute R_ab = 2K h_ab, R = 6K into Riemann-from-Ricci (24.24) to get constant curvature (24.23).
Solve lambda'/r = 2K e^lambda to get e^{-lambda} = 1 - K r^2 (24.28).
Coordinate change r = rbar/(1 + K rbar^2/4) gives conformally flat form (24.31).

sections.title: The geometry of 3-spaces of constant curvature
sections.summary: Case by case: for k = +1, r = sin chi gives R_0^2[d chi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2], embedded as the 3-sphere w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2 = R_0^2 in Euclidean 4-space; geodesic 2-spheres have area 4 pi R_0^2 sin^2 chi (growing then shrinking to zero at the antipode), total volume 2 pi^2 R_0^3, closed topology, spacetime R x S^3. The embedding is a visual aid only; the physical space has no outside. For k = 0 the slice is Euclidean R^3, open topology. For k = -1, r = sinh chi gives a hyperboloid w^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 = R_0^2 in Minkowski 4-space; sphere areas grow like sinh^2 chi, faster than flat, with infinite volume. Other topologies from identifications are possible but not pursued.
key_moves: Coordinate r = sin chi removes the coordinate singularity at r = 1.
Explicit embedding (24.41) and constraint (24.42).
Area A_chi and volume 2 pi^2 R_0^3 integrals.
Proper radial coordinate r' = R_0 chi: area close to 4 pi r'^2 for small r', then falls below it.
k = -1 needs a Lorentzian ambient space (24.46)-(24.48).
Topology: R x S^3 (closed) or R^4 (open), simplest choices only.

sections.title: Friedmann's equation
sections.summary: Combines the Robertson-Walker metric, a perfect fluid comoving with u^a = (1,0,0,0), and G_ab - Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab to obtain two independent equations. The first-order one is read as an energy integral and the second-order one as an equation of motion. Differentiating and combining yields d(rho R^3)/dt + p d(R^3)/dt = 0, i.e. dE + p dV = 0, equivalent to T^{ab}_{;b} = 0 via the Bianchi identities. Eliminating the curvature term gives Rddot/R = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p - Lambda/4 pi); if the bracket is positive and the universe expands now, the concave graph of R(t) must hit zero in the finite past (FRW singularity theorem; with Lambda = 0 the condition is the strong energy condition). With p about 1e-5 to 1e-6 of rho, dust is adopted; integration gives the conserved C = 8 pi R^3 rho/3 and Friedmann's equation Rdot^2 = C/R + Lambda R^2/3 - k, identical to the Newtonian analogue.
key_moves: Field equations reduce to (24.52) and (24.53); rho and p depend only on t.
Combine derivative of (24.52) with (24.53) to get (24.54).
Interpret as first law dE + p dV = 0 with V proportional to R^3.
Acceleration equation from a linear combination of (24.52) and (24.53).
Concavity plus present expansion => R = 0 at finite past time.
Dust: (24.53) integrates to (24.58); constant fixed by (24.52) as (24.59).
Friedmann's equation (24.60) matches (24.17).

sections.title: Propagation of light
sections.summary: Places the observer at r = 0 and follows radial null geodesics: dt/R = +/- dr/sqrt(1-kr^2). The comoving coordinate of a source is a fixed function f(r_1) of the integral of dt/R between emission and reception, so two successive signals satisfy dt_0/R(t_0) = dt_1/R(t_1). Since t is proper time for fundamental observers, received periods are stretched by R(t_0)/R(t_1), giving 1+z = R(t_0)/R(t_1): redshift for expansion, blueshift for contraction, which the authors warn is a different thing from the special-relativistic Doppler effect. For nearby sources z ~ Rdot(t_0) r_1, a linear redshift-distance relation.
key_moves: Null condition in RW metric (24.61).
Integral of dt/R equals f(r_1) = arcsin r_1, r_1, arcsinh r_1 (24.62)-(24.63).
Subtract integrals for two successive rays; take R outside tiny intervals (24.64).
Proper-time interpretation gives frequency ratio (24.65) and redshift (24.66).
First-order Taylor expansion gives z ~ H dt and dt ~ R r_1, hence (24.68).

sections.title: A cosmological definition of distance
sections.summary: Cosmic time allows a clean absolute distance: the geodesic length within a slice between two fundamental particles, R(t) times the comoving radial integral, but it is not measurable. An observational distance from known physical size and measured angular size needs the true size. Instead a luminosity-based distance is used: in an expanding universe the arrival rate of photons and the energy of each photon both drop by 1+z, motivating d_L^2 = E/(4 pi I (1+z)^2). Mentions apparent magnitude (logarithmic in received energy), the problem of unknown intrinsic luminosity, evolution of galaxies, standard candles (Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae) and calibration.
key_moves: Absolute distance from dt = d theta = d phi = 0 (24.69).
Size over angle definition (24.70).
Two separate (1+z) dimming factors: time dilation of arrivals and photon energy loss.
Luminosity distance (24.71).
m = const - 0.4 log E_R; standard candles and calibration problem.

sections.title: Hubble's law in relativistic cosmology
sections.summary: Light emitted at P_1 is spread at reception time over a sphere through O_0 whose area, by homogeneity, equals that of the sphere of coordinate radius r_1 around O_0, namely 4 pi R_0^2 r_1^2; with the two (1+z) factors this gives d_L = r_1 R(t_0). Combining with z ~ Rdot_0 r_1 yields Hubble's law z ~ H_0 d_L, now deduced rather than assumed. Hubble time T_0 = 1/H_0 is about 1e10 years, and when rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi the age is less than T_0. Defines the deceleration parameter q = -R Rddot/Rdot^2 (measured q_0 about -0.6 +/- 0.3, accelerating), gives the second-order law d_L = z T_0[1 - (1+q_0)z/2], shows Sandage's 1970 redshift-magnitude data, and derives q = (4 pi rho/3 - Lambda/3)/H^2.
key_moves: Homogeneity swaps the sphere centred on P_0 for one centred on O_0.
Area 4 pi R_0^2 r_1^2 from RW angular part; flux with (1+z)^2 gives (24.72).
Hubble law (24.74) from (24.68) and (24.72).
Age bound via Fig. 24.8 when deceleration holds.
Deceleration parameter (24.76) and its measured sign.
Second-order expansion (24.78); dependence on q_0 visible in Fig. 24.13.
Differentiate Friedmann's equation to obtain (24.79).

concepts.name: cosmology
concepts.definition: The study of the large-scale structure and dynamics of the universe treated as a single physical system, usually after averaging away galaxies, clusters and smaller structure.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening framing of the chapter; contrasted with laboratory physics because the system is unique and experiments cannot be repeated.

concepts.name: fluid (smoothing) approximation
concepts.definition: Modelling the matter of the universe as a continuous distribution obtained by averaging over regions large enough (in the book, cells over about 1e9 light years) to contain many clusters, so that homogeneity can hold on average though not in detail.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the start as smoothing out all irregularities, and later quantified when explaining in what sense the universe is homogeneous (like a gas).
concepts.notes: The book compares this to the homogeneity of a gas.

concepts.name: uniqueness of the universe
concepts.definition: The epistemic point that cosmology studies a single system which cannot be re-run under controlled conditions, so models must rely on extrapolating locally verified physics plus simplicity assumptions.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised in the preview and again as Weyl's motivation for privileged observers.

concepts.name: hot big bang model
concepts.definition: The model in which the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state (a singularity in classical models); as it cooled, particles, light nuclei and atoms formed, then stars and galaxies.
concepts.how_introduced: Described qualitatively in the preview as the model favoured since the 1960s; supported later by the CMB and by the FRW singularity theorem.
concepts.notes: The book attributes a success to predicted heavy-element abundances; modern big-bang nucleosynthesis concerns light elements (H, He, Li); heavy elements are made in stars.

concepts.name: perfect cosmological principle
concepts.definition: A strengthened simplicity assumption: the large-scale universe is unchanging not only from place to place but also from epoch to epoch, so no location and no time is special.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the preview as the basis of the steady-state school and as leading to de Sitter spacetime.

concepts.name: steady-state theory
concepts.definition: A non-Friedmann cosmology based on the perfect cosmological principle, in which the universe expands but its large-scale appearance never changes; now rejected observationally.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical aside in the preview; treated properly in §25.6.

concepts.name: de Sitter solution
concepts.definition: A maximally symmetric vacuum solution with positive cosmological constant, important as an alternative asymptotic structure to Minkowski space.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the preview as the outcome of the perfect cosmological principle; deferred to Chapter 25.

concepts.name: Olbers' paradox
concepts.definition: The contradiction between the dark night sky and the prediction that a static, infinite, eternal universe uniformly filled with stars would have a sky everywhere as bright as the surface of a star.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivating puzzle of §24.2: equal-intensity shells argument, then occultation, thermodynamic equilibrium and line-of-sight versions, then attempted and accepted resolutions.
concepts.notes: The book gives two escapes. (i) A young universe in which stars switched on recently: the book notes that making this short enough can conflict with the ages of the oldest stars. (ii) Expansion, where redshift drains energy from distant light; the book calls this the accepted resolution. Modern analyses (e.g. Harrison) find that finite age and finite stellar lifetimes are the dominant factor.

concepts.name: lookback time
concepts.definition: Because light travels at finite speed, observing more distant sources means seeing them as they were at earlier cosmic times.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in the Olbers discussion to allow luminosity to vary with time, and later in the world-picture concept and the evolution caveat for standard candles.

concepts.name: Newtonian cosmology
concepts.definition: A model of the universe using Newtonian gravity plus ad hoc symmetry assumptions (and optionally a cosmological force proportional to distance) that reproduces the form of Friedmann's equation, though the interpretation of its terms differs.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from n point galaxies moving radially about an origin; energy conservation gives the scale-factor ODE.
concepts.notes: The book stresses it came historically after GR and applies only to a finite, arbitrarily large system.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
concepts.definition: A constant Lambda entering Einstein's equations as G_ab - Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab; in the Newtonian analogue it corresponds to a force Lambda m r/3 that repels (Lambda>0) or attracts (Lambda<0) in proportion to distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an extra force in the Newtonian model, cited in the preview as a possible cosmic-scale interaction, and included in the relativistic field equations of §24.9.

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: A universal function of cosmic time by which all separations between comoving particles (or the spatial metric) are multiplied; ratios of its values at two times give the magnification of the spatial geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: First as S(t) in the Newtonian model (uniform scaling is the only motion compatible with homogeneity), then as S^2(t) multiplying h_{alpha beta} via the similar-triangle argument, then renormalized to R(t).
concepts.notes: Two normalizations: S(t) with curvature K, or R(t) with k = +1, 0, -1.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional expansion rate H = Rdot/R (or Sdot/S), with dimensions of inverse time.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in the Newtonian model as the proportionality constant between recession speed and distance, redefined in relativistic form in §24.12.

concepts.name: Hubble constant
concepts.definition: The present-epoch value of the Hubble parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Named right after Newtonian Hubble's law; numerically discussed via the Hubble time in §24.12.

concepts.name: Hubble's law
concepts.definition: For nearby galaxies at a given epoch, recession velocity (or redshift) is proportional to distance: v = H r in the Newtonian model, z ~ H_0 d_L to first order in relativistic cosmology.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived kinematically from uniform scaling in §24.3, then deduced in §24.12 from null geodesics and the luminosity distance without assuming velocities.
concepts.notes: Exercise 24.4 shows Hubble's law and uniform scaling are equivalent in the Newtonian model.

concepts.name: curvature index k
concepts.definition: The sign of the spatial curvature after rescaling the radial coordinate and scale factor: +1 for closed spherical slices, 0 for flat, -1 for hyperbolic; in the Newtonian analogue it is minus the sign of total energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears first as the normalized energy constant k = -mu^2 E/A in the Newtonian model, then as K/|K| in the Robertson-Walker metric.

concepts.name: big crunch
concepts.definition: A possible future in which expansion halts and reverses so the universe collapses to a final singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a question arising from the Newtonian energy equation; answered in Chapter 25.

concepts.name: cosmological principle
concepts.definition: The assumption that, once local lumps are smoothed out, every observer at a given cosmic time sees the same large-scale universe as every other; geometrically, spacetime is sliced into spacelike hypersurfaces each of which is homogeneous and isotropic about all of its points.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a highlighted principle, motivated by the Copernican principle, made precise via isometries, supported by CMB isotropy, and finally adopted on pragmatic grounds.

concepts.name: Copernican principle
concepts.definition: The idea that we (Earth, solar system, galaxy, local group) do not occupy a specially privileged position.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the conceptual ancestor of the cosmological principle.

concepts.name: homogeneity
concepts.definition: A spatial slice is called homogeneous when its isometry group acts transitively: for any two of its points some symmetry of the slice's metric sends one to the other, so no location is geometrically special.
concepts.how_introduced: Formal definition accompanying Fig. 24.2 (an isometry arrow mapping one point to another within a slice).

concepts.name: isotropy
concepts.definition: A manifold is isotropic about a point if no direction there is distinguished (it is spherically symmetric about that point); globally isotropic if this holds at every point, which implies homogeneity.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §24.4 and used in §24.7 through the eigenvector argument on the Einstein tensor.

concepts.name: cosmic time
concepts.definition: A time coordinate t whose constant-t slices are the homogeneous, isotropic hypersurfaces orthogonal to the fundamental observers' world-lines; it coincides with the proper time of those observers and defines a cosmic notion of simultaneity.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed when formulating the cosmological principle and constructed explicitly in §24.6 from hypersurface-orthogonal geodesics; shown to be proper time in §24.10.

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: A nearly isotropic bath of blackbody radiation at about 2.7 K pervading the universe, interpreted as the cooled thermal relic of the hot big bang.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as the strongest evidence for isotropy (Penzias and Wilson 1965; Planck isotropy to about 1 part in 1e5).

concepts.name: Bianchi models
concepts.definition: Cosmologies whose slices are homogeneous under a three-dimensional transformation group but not isotropic; classified into types I to IX, with field equations reducing to ODEs in time.
concepts.how_introduced: Survey of alternatives to the cosmological principle in §24.4.

concepts.name: Kasner solution
concepts.definition: The vacuum Bianchi type I metric dt^2 - t^{2p1}dx^2 - t^{2p2}dy^2 - t^{2p3}dz^2 with sum p_i = sum p_i^2 = 1, leaving one free parameter; it expands in some directions while contracting in another.
concepts.how_introduced: Example of an anisotropic model and of cigar/pancake singularity structure.

concepts.name: cigar and pancake singularities
concepts.definition: Anisotropic initial singularities in which a small initially spherical region becomes infinitely long and thin (cigar) or collapses to an infinitely thin disc (pancake) as t -> 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Described for Kasner and matter Bianchi models as the generic physical (density-divergent) singularities.

concepts.name: whimper singularity
concepts.definition: A weaker singularity where curvature components are unbounded in a parallelly propagated orthonormal frame along a curve reaching it, while bounded in some other frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a special non-generic case among Bianchi models.

concepts.name: BKL singularity
concepts.definition: The analysis by Belinski, Khalatnikov and Lifshitz suggesting that a generic cosmological singularity is far more complex than the isotropic point-like Friedmann singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: One of three reasons given for studying anisotropic models.

concepts.name: hierarchical cosmology
concepts.definition: Charlier's 1908 proposal that matter is organized in an unending hierarchy of clusters, so no smooth average density exists.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a radical alternative; observational superclustering is said to stop at clusters of clusters.

concepts.name: Weyl's postulate
concepts.definition: Robertson's version of Weyl's assumption: the world-lines of the smoothed-out galaxies form a family of timelike geodesics, one through each event, which fan out from a common origin in the past (possibly infinitely far back) and meet nowhere else except perhaps at a final singular point. Hence the matter has a single well-defined 4-velocity everywhere.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by how a covariant theory can describe a unique universe; stated in Robertson's form as a highlighted postulate.

concepts.name: substratum
concepts.definition: The idealized fluid filling space whose particles are the smoothed-out galaxies; its world-lines define privileged observers who see the universe as isotropic.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by Weyl's reasoning that local peculiar velocities are small compared with the general motion.

concepts.name: timelike geodesic congruence
concepts.definition: A family of timelike geodesics such that exactly one passes through each point of the region considered.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in stating Weyl's postulate; the no-intersection property gives a unique velocity field.

concepts.name: perfect fluid
concepts.definition: Matter described by T_ab = (rho + p)u_a u_b - p g_ab with energy density rho, isotropic pressure p and a single 4-velocity field u^a.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by Weyl's postulate (unique velocity at each event) and used as the source in the Friedmann equations.

concepts.name: standard models of relativistic cosmology
concepts.definition: Cosmological models built on three assumptions: the cosmological principle, Weyl's postulate, and general relativity (with cosmological term).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the three ingredients at the start of §24.6 and restated in §24.9.

concepts.name: hypersurface-orthogonal congruence
aliases: orthogonality of substratum world-lines to slices
concepts.definition: In a cosmology obeying the cosmological principle and Weyl's postulate, the substratum world-lines are orthogonal to the homogeneous slices, since any tilt would single out a spatial direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Isotropy argument at the start of §24.6, drawn in Fig. 24.3 with right-angle marks.

concepts.name: comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: Spatial coordinates that are constant along each fundamental particle's world-line, so galaxies keep fixed coordinate labels while the scale factor changes physical separations.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed together with cosmic time from the orthogonal geodesic congruence.

concepts.name: world map
concepts.definition: The distribution of events on a surface of constant cosmic time, i.e. the universe 'as it is now' everywhere simultaneously.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined using cosmic simultaneity and drawn in Figs. 24.3-24.4.

concepts.name: world picture
concepts.definition: The set of events an observer actually sees at an instant, lying on that observer's past light cone, so more distant events are seen at earlier cosmic times.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the world map in Fig. 24.4.

concepts.name: space of constant curvature
concepts.definition: A (pseudo-)Riemannian space whose curvature tensor has the form R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc) with constant K, so every point and 2-plane has the same sectional curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Required for slices that are homogeneous and isotropic; derived for three dimensions from isotropy in §24.7.

concepts.name: Einstein space
concepts.definition: A space whose Ricci tensor is a constant multiple of the metric, R_ab = lambda g_ab (a name the authors call somewhat confusing).
concepts.how_introduced: Shown to follow from isotropy about every point via the eigenvector argument on G^a_b and the contracted Bianchi identities.

concepts.name: Riemann tensor determined by Ricci in three dimensions
concepts.definition: In three dimensions the Weyl tensor vanishes identically, so the full Riemann tensor is an algebraic function of the Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §6.13 and (6.88) to show a 3D Einstein space has constant curvature.

concepts.name: conformally flat metric
concepts.definition: A metric that is a position-dependent multiple of a flat metric; the constant-curvature 3-metric takes this form in the barred radial coordinate.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by the substitution r = rbar/(1 + K rbar^2/4).

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.definition: The most general spacetime metric compatible with the cosmological principle and comoving cosmic time: ds^2 = dt^2 - R^2(t)[dr^2/(1-kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2], k = +1, 0, -1 (equivalently in conformally flat barred form).
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from the separable form (24.19) and the constant-curvature 3-metric, then normalized.
concepts.notes: The book attaches the name specifically to the barred (conformally flat) form (24.37).

concepts.name: 3-sphere
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional analogue of a sphere: the set w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2 = R_0^2 in Euclidean 4-space, with metric R_0^2[d chi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2], finite volume 2 pi^2 R_0^3 and no boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by r = sin chi for k = +1 and visualized by an embedding with one dimension suppressed (Fig. 24.5).

concepts.name: closed universe
concepts.definition: A cosmological model whose spatial slices are compact (for k = +1, 3-spheres), so the spacetime has topology R x S^3 and radial geodesics return to their starting point.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after the S^3 computation; drawn as a cylinder in Fig. 24.6.

concepts.name: flat space (k=0)
concepts.definition: The k = 0 case in which each slice is ordinary Euclidean 3-space, infinite in extent, with spacetime topology R^4 (called open).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by ordinary Cartesian substitution in (24.38).

concepts.name: hyperbolic 3-space
concepts.definition: The negatively curved space of constant curvature, realized as the hyperboloid w^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 = R_0^2 in 4D Minkowski space, with metric R_0^2[d chi^2 + sinh^2 chi dOmega^2] and infinite volume.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by r = sinh chi; requires a Lorentzian ambient space for the embedding (Fig. 24.7).

concepts.name: embedding diagram
concepts.definition: A visualization in which a curved space (with some dimensions suppressed) is drawn as a surface in a higher-dimensional flat space whose induced metric reproduces the original geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Used for k = +1 (Euclidean R^4) and k = -1 (Minkowski R^{1,3}), with an explicit caution that the ambient space has no physical meaning.

concepts.name: radius of the universe
concepts.definition: For the closed model, the scale factor R(t_0) equals the radius of the embedded 3-sphere, since the total volume is 2 pi^2 R^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after computing the S^3 volume.

concepts.name: spatial topology of cosmological models
concepts.definition: The global shape of the spatial slices; the simplest choices are S^3 (closed) for k = +1 and R^3 (open) for k = 0, -1, but identifications can produce other topologies with the same local geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after each case in §24.8 with a note that other topologies are possible but not studied.

concepts.name: Friedmann equations
concepts.definition: The two independent components of Einstein's equations for a Robertson-Walker metric with a comoving perfect fluid and Lambda: 3(Rdot^2+k)/R^2 - Lambda = 8 pi rho and (2R Rddot + Rdot^2 + k)/R^2 - Lambda = -8 pi p.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived (as an exercise) by inserting the three ingredients; the first read as an energy integral, the second as an equation of motion.

concepts.name: energy conservation in cosmology
aliases: first law for the expanding universe
concepts.definition: For a comoving volume V proportional to R^3 containing energy E = rho V, the field equations imply dE + p dV = 0: pressure does work as the universe expands; this is the content of T^{ab}_{;b} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating the first Friedmann equation and combining with the second; then identified with the conservation law guaranteed by the contracted Bianchi identities.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: The identity G^{ab}_{;b} = 0 (and hence (G^{ab} - Lambda g^{ab})_{;b} = 0), which forces the source to satisfy T^{ab}_{;b} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled to explain why the Friedmann equations contain energy conservation, and used to show K is constant in G_ab = -K g_ab.

concepts.name: acceleration equation
concepts.definition: The combination of the two Friedmann equations from which both Rdot and the curvature index k drop out: Rddot/R = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p - Lambda/4 pi). Density and pressure (through rho + 3p) slow the expansion, while a positive Lambda speeds it up.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by a linear combination of (24.52) and (24.53) to motivate the singularity theorem.
concepts.notes: The book's instruction for forming the combination has the roles swapped (see gaps). The reading copy also lost overdots on this page ('eliminate R', 'so that R < 0'); the render of pdf p.500 shows Rdot and Rddot.

concepts.name: strong energy condition
concepts.definition: For a perfect fluid, the requirement rho + 3p >= 0 (together with rho + p >= 0), meaning gravity is attractive for timelike congruences.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified as the Lambda = 0 version of the condition for guaranteed deceleration.

concepts.name: FRW singularity theorem
concepts.definition: If Lambda = 0 and rho + 3p > 0 (more generally rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi) and the universe is expanding today, then R(t) vanished at a finite time in the past: there was an initial big bang singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Proved graphically: Rddot < 0 means the graph of R lies below each tangent; the present tangent crosses the t axis at finite time, so R must reach zero even sooner (Fig. 24.8).

concepts.name: dust
concepts.definition: A perfect fluid with p = 0, appropriate for the present universe where pressure is about 1e-5 to 1e-6 of the matter energy density.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted in §24.9 after estimating the pressure-to-density ratio, turning (24.54) into mass conservation.

concepts.name: Friedmann's equation
concepts.definition: For pressure-free matter, Rdot^2 = C/R + Lambda R^2/3 - k with C = (8 pi/3) rho R^3 constant; its solutions are the Friedmann models.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by integrating the second Friedmann equation with p = 0 and fixing the constant from the first; noted to coincide with the Newtonian result (24.17).

concepts.name: Friedmann models
concepts.definition: The family of homogeneous isotropic cosmologies obtained by solving Friedmann's equation for different k, Lambda and C.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the preview and at the end of §24.9; solved in Chapter 25.

concepts.name: big bang
concepts.definition: The finite-past event at which the scale factor vanishes and density diverges in Friedmann models satisfying the singularity theorem conditions.
concepts.how_introduced: Qualitative in the preview; made precise via the FRW singularity theorem.

concepts.name: radial null geodesic
concepts.definition: A light ray moving at fixed theta and phi; in the Robertson-Walker metric it obeys dt/R(t) = +/- dr/sqrt(1-kr^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Set ds = d theta = d phi = 0 with the observer at the origin (allowed by homogeneity).

concepts.name: comoving distance function f(r)
concepts.definition: The dimensionless comoving radial distance f(r_1) = arcsin r_1, r_1, or arcsinh r_1 (for k = +1, 0, -1), equal to the integral of dt/R along a radial light ray from the source to the observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Result of integrating the null condition (24.62)-(24.63).

concepts.name: cosmological redshift
concepts.definition: The fractional decrease in frequency of light from a comoving source, 1+z = R(t_0)/R(t_1), due to the change in scale factor between emission and reception; a blueshift in a contracting universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from two successive null rays and the proper-time meaning of t (Fig. 24.10); distinguished from the special-relativistic Doppler effect.

concepts.name: proper distance
concepts.definition: The geodesic length within a slice of constant cosmic time between two fundamental particles: R(t) times the comoving radial integral.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the mathematically natural distance and immediately set aside as unmeasurable (Fig. 24.11).
concepts.notes: The book's d_A means absolute distance, not the angular-diameter distance usually denoted d_A today.

concepts.name: angular-size distance
concepts.definition: A distance defined by the ratio of an object's true linear diameter to its observed angular diameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as an operational alternative but rejected because true sizes are unknown.

concepts.name: luminosity distance
concepts.definition: A distance inferred from how bright a source of known power appears; in the book it is defined with the redshift losses divided out, d_L^2 = E/(4 pi I (1+z)^2), which in a Robertson-Walker universe gives d_L = r_1 R(t_0).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by counting two (1+z) losses (arrival rate and photon energy), then computed from the area of the sphere over which light spreads by the time of reception (Fig. 24.12).
concepts.notes: Modern convention defines d_L^2 = E/(4 pi I), giving d_L = (1+z) r_1 R(t_0); the book's d_L equals the modern transverse comoving distance.

concepts.name: apparent magnitude
concepts.definition: A logarithmic brightness scale for received energy, m = constant - 0.4 log10 E_R (brighter objects have smaller m).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned loosely as the astronomers' unit; used on the axis of Fig. 24.13.

concepts.name: standard candles
concepts.definition: Classes of sources believed to have nearly the same intrinsic luminosity at all places and times (e.g. Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae), allowing luminosity distances once calibrated.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after noting galaxies evolve, so they are unreliable as equal-luminosity sources.

concepts.name: galaxy evolution
concepts.definition: Distant galaxies are seen when younger, so their average luminosity need not equal that of nearby galaxies, biasing distance estimates that assume equal luminosity.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a flaw in treating all galaxies as equally luminous.

concepts.name: Hubble time
concepts.definition: The reciprocal of the Hubble constant, a characteristic expansion timescale; for a decelerating universe it is an upper bound on the age.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined after Hubble's law; the book quotes about 1e10 years within a factor of 2.

concepts.name: age of the universe
concepts.definition: The cosmic time elapsed since R = 0; if rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi throughout, it is less than the Hubble time.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off Fig. 24.8: the tangent at t_0 meets the axis a Hubble time earlier, the curve meets it later.

concepts.name: deceleration parameter
concepts.definition: The dimensionless quantity q = -R Rddot/Rdot^2: positive when expansion slows, negative when it speeds up; related to density and Lambda by q = (4 pi rho/3 - Lambda/3)/H^2 for dust.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §24.12, given observational value about -0.6 +/- 0.3, used in the second-order Hubble law, and linked to Friedmann's equation.

concepts.name: second-order Hubble law
concepts.definition: Expanding the scale factor to second order around t_0 gives d_L = z T_0 [1 - (1+q_0) z/2 + ...] (with the book's d_L), so deviations from linearity at larger z measure q_0.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with derivation left to Exercise 24.17 (trapezium rule); compared with Sandage's data (Fig. 24.13).
concepts.notes: With the modern luminosity distance the bracket is [1 + (1-q_0)z/2].

concepts.name: peculiar velocities
concepts.definition: Motions of galaxies relative to the smoothed Hubble flow, below about 1e-3 c, which dominate the observed redshift of very nearby galaxies.
concepts.how_introduced: Neglected in Weyl's postulate; revisited as the reason Hubble's law fails for the closest objects.

concepts.name: dominant energy condition
concepts.definition: The requirement from Chapter 12 that the cosmic fluid be physically reasonable: energy density non-negative and energy flux never spacelike, which for a perfect fluid means rho >= |p|.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed in passing, right after the two Friedmann equations, as an extra condition that rho and p must satisfy; the stronger-looking condition rho + 3p > 0 used for the singularity theorem is then identified separately as the strong energy condition.
concepts.notes: Dominant and strong conditions are logically independent; learners often conflate them.

key_equations.name: Olbers shell contribution
key_equations.meaning: A thin shell of stars contributes an intensity at its centre independent of its radius, so an infinite static universe gives a divergent (or, with occultation, stellar-surface) brightness.
key_equations.symbols: \ell: number density of stars times mean luminosity; r, dr: shell radius and thickness

key_equations.name: radial motion
key_equations.meaning: Spherical symmetry about O forces purely radial motion of each galaxy.

key_equations.name: Newtonian potential energy
key_equations.meaning: Total gravitational potential energy, each pair counted once.

key_equations.name: cosmological force
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian stand-in for the cosmological term: a force proportional to distance from O, repulsive for Lambda>0.

key_equations.name: cosmological potential energy
key_equations.meaning: Potential whose negative gradient gives (24.4).

key_equations.name: total energy
key_equations.latex: E=\tfrac12\sum_i m_i\dot r_i^2-G\sum_{i<j}\frac{m_im_j}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j|}-\tfrac16\Lambda\sum_i m_ir_i^2
key_equations.meaning: Conserved total energy of the discrete Newtonian model.

key_equations.name: uniform scaling
key_equations.meaning: The only motion compatible with homogeneity and isotropy is a common rescaling of all distances.
Velocity of each galaxy follows from differentiating the scaling law.

key_equations.name: Hubble parameter
key_equations.meaning: Fractional expansion rate, units of inverse time.

key_equations.name: Hubble's law (Newtonian)
key_equations.meaning: Recession speed proportional to distance at a given epoch.

key_equations.name: Newtonian cosmological energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Energy conservation in terms of the scale factor alone; with Lambda=0, expansion lowers |potential| so kinetic term must fall: deceleration.

key_equations.name: coefficients
key_equations.latex: A=\tfrac12\sum_i m_i r_i(t_0)^2,\quad B=G\sum_{i<j}\frac{m_im_j}{|\mathbf r_i(t_0)-\mathbf r_j(t_0)|},\quad D=\tfrac16\Lambda\sum_i m_ir_i(t_0)^2=\tfrac13\Lambda A
key_equations.meaning: Constants fixed by the configuration at the reference epoch; A is half the moment of inertia about O.
Energy equation solved for the expansion rate.
Rescaling the scale factor by a constant.

key_equations.name: Newtonian Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian model yields exactly the form of the relativistic Friedmann equation; k is minus the sign of the total energy.

key_equations.name: normalization
key_equations.meaning: Choice of mu making k = +1 or -1; mu arbitrary if E = 0 (k = 0).

key_equations.name: Kasner metric
key_equations.meaning: Vacuum Bianchi I anisotropic cosmology with one free exponent; singular at t = 0 with cigar or pancake behaviour.

key_equations.name: synchronous comoving form
key_equations.meaning: Consequence of orthogonal geodesic congruence: cosmic time with no cross terms.

key_equations.name: separable spatial metric
key_equations.meaning: Time enters the spatial metric only as an overall magnification, required by similar-triangle evolution.

key_equations.name: constant curvature
key_equations.meaning: Defining property of a space of constant curvature K.

key_equations.name: isotropy condition on Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: No preferred eigen-directions forces G to be a multiple of the metric; Bianchi identities make K constant.

key_equations.name: Einstein space
key_equations.meaning: Isotropy about every point implies an Einstein space in any dimension n>2.

key_equations.name: 3D constant curvature
key_equations.meaning: In 3D an Einstein space has constant curvature.

key_equations.name: 3D Riemann from Ricci
key_equations.meaning: Vanishing Weyl tensor in 3D; substituting R_{alpha beta} = 2K h, R = 6K gives (24.23).

key_equations.name: spherically symmetric 3-metric
key_equations.meaning: Ansatz justified by isotropy about the origin.

key_equations.name: Ricci components
key_equations.meaning: Non-zero Ricci components of the ansatz (24.25), written here in corrected form. The printed line (checked on the page render) lists R_22 as cosec^2 theta and attaches the bracketed expression to R_33, a misprint; (24.27) only makes sense if that expression is the theta-theta component, with the phi-phi one carrying an extra sin^2 theta.
Einstein-space condition R_{alpha beta} = 2K h_{alpha beta} applied to (24.26).
Solution of (24.27).

key_equations.name: constant-curvature 3-metric
key_equations.meaning: Spatial geometry of homogeneous isotropic slices.

key_equations.name: conformally flat form
key_equations.latex: r=\frac{\bar r}{1+\frac14K\bar r^2},\qquad d\sigma^2=\frac{d\bar r^2+\bar r^2d\Omega^2}{(1+\frac14K\bar r^2)^2}
key_equations.meaning: Change of radial coordinate displaying the 3-metric as conformal to flat space.
Cosmological line element before normalizing K.

key_equations.name: rescaled radial coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Absorbing |K| into the coordinate leaves only its sign k.

key_equations.name: normalized scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Definition of R(t).

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element (unbarred)
key_equations.meaning: The standard metric of homogeneous isotropic cosmology, k = +1, 0, -1.
key_equations.symbols: r dimensionless comoving radial coordinate; R has dimensions of length

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element (barred)
key_equations.meaning: Conformally flat form, the one the book names Robertson-Walker; repeated as (24.49).

key_equations.name: slice geometry
key_equations.meaning: Geometry of the slice t = t_0.

key_equations.name: 3-sphere metric
key_equations.meaning: k = +1 slice in hyperspherical coordinates, regular at r = 1.

key_equations.name: 3-sphere embedding
key_equations.meaning: The k = +1 slice is a round 3-sphere in Euclidean 4-space.

key_equations.name: geodesic 2-sphere area (k=+1)
key_equations.meaning: Area of spheres at proper radius r' = R_0 chi grows, peaks at the equator, returns to zero at the antipode.

key_equations.name: volume of the 3-sphere
key_equations.meaning: Finite spatial volume of the closed universe; motivates calling R the radius of the universe.

key_equations.name: flat slice
key_equations.meaning: k = 0 slice is Euclidean. The printed third substitution reads x = R_0 r cos theta; it should be z.

key_equations.name: hyperbolic 3-metric
key_equations.meaning: k = -1 slice in hyperbolic coordinates.

key_equations.name: hyperboloid embedding
key_equations.meaning: The k = -1 slice is one sheet of a hyperboloid in Minkowski 4-space (signature +2 ambient metric).

key_equations.name: geodesic 2-sphere area (k=-1)
key_equations.meaning: Area grows exponentially for large chi, faster than in flat space; volume is infinite.

key_equations.name: perfect fluid
key_equations.meaning: Source demanded by Weyl's postulate, comoving in cosmic-time coordinates.

key_equations.name: field equations with Lambda
key_equations.meaning: Einstein's equations in relativistic units with cosmological term.

key_equations.name: first Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Energy-type constraint relating expansion rate, curvature, Lambda and density.

key_equations.name: second Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Equation of motion for the scale factor involving pressure.

key_equations.name: intermediate continuity step
key_equations.meaning: Time derivative of (24.52) combined with (24.53).

key_equations.name: continuity equation
key_equations.meaning: Energy conservation for a comoving volume.

key_equations.name: first law
key_equations.meaning: With E = rho V and V proportional to R^3: pressure does work in the expansion.

key_equations.name: conservation law
key_equations.meaning: Same content as (24.55), guaranteed by the contracted Bianchi identities.

key_equations.name: acceleration equation
key_equations.meaning: Deceleration from rho + 3p, acceleration from positive Lambda. Obtained as 3 x (24.53) minus (24.52); the text's verbal recipe reverses the roles.

key_equations.name: dust
key_equations.meaning: Present-epoch approximation (p/rho about 1e-5 to 1e-6).

key_equations.name: first integral for dust
key_equations.meaning: Integral of (24.53) with p = 0; C is twice the Euclidean mass of a sphere of radius R.

key_equations.name: Friedmann's equation
key_equations.meaning: Governing ODE for the scale factor of pressure-free models; identical in form to (24.17).

key_equations.name: radial null geodesic
key_equations.meaning: Light-ray equation in RW, plus for outgoing, minus for incoming.

key_equations.name: comoving distance of source
key_equations.meaning: The conformal-time interval of a ray equals a fixed function of the source's comoving coordinate.
Successive signals: received interval stretched by the expansion factor.

key_equations.name: cosmological redshift
key_equations.meaning: Redshift measures the ratio of scale factors at reception and emission.
First-order redshift for nearby sources.

key_equations.name: linear redshift-distance relation
key_equations.meaning: Nearby: redshift proportional to comoving coordinate distance.

key_equations.name: absolute distance
key_equations.meaning: Proper distance at fixed cosmic time.

key_equations.name: observational (angular-size) distance
key_equations.meaning: True diameter over angular diameter.

key_equations.name: luminosity distance (book's definition)
key_equations.meaning: Flux-based distance with both redshift dimming factors removed.
key_equations.symbols: E: emitted power; I: received flux

key_equations.name: apparent magnitude
key_equations.meaning: Logarithmic brightness scale.

key_equations.name: received flux in RW
key_equations.meaning: Energy spread over a sphere of area 4 pi R_0^2 r_1^2, reduced twice by (1+z).

key_equations.name: luminosity distance in RW
key_equations.meaning: With the book's definition, d_L equals present-day areal radius of the sphere through the observer.

key_equations.name: relativistic Hubble law
key_equations.meaning: Hubble's law deduced to first order.

key_equations.name: Hubble time
key_equations.meaning: Book's quoted value, uncertain by a factor of 2.

key_equations.name: deceleration parameter
key_equations.meaning: Dimensionless measure of deceleration.
Quoted observational value: the expansion is accelerating.

key_equations.name: second-order Hubble law
key_equations.meaning: Curvature of the redshift-distance relation measures q_0 (book's d_L; modern d_L has 1 + (1-q_0)z/2).

key_equations.name: q from dynamics
key_equations.meaning: Links deceleration, expansion rate, mean density and Lambda for dust models.

figures.label: Fig. 24.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A star's light toward P is blocked by a nearer star.
figures.visual_description: Two small outlined five-pointed stars joined by a straight line: the upper-right star emits along the line, an arrowhead points down-left toward the lower-left star, which lies between it and the observer. On the rendered page a dot labelled P sits further down-left (the exported image crops out P, which the inventory caption records only as 'P').
figures.what_it_teaches: Occultation: in an infinite static starry universe, far-away stars are hidden behind nearer ones, which caps the divergent shell sum at the surface brightness of a star rather than infinity.

redesign.idea: Olbers sky simulator: a 2D (or 3D fly-through) random star field around an observer where sightlines are cast in every direction; the rendered sky fills in as the universe gets older or larger.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for star density, universe age (light-travel horizon), and expansion redshift factor; toggles for 'static' vs 'expanding' and for occultation. A readout plots sky brightness vs age and the fraction of sightlines ending on a star.

figures.label: Fig. 24.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spacetime cut into a stack of homogeneous spatial slices.
figures.visual_description: Three overlapping parallelograms stacked obliquely, labelled t = t_1 (front, lowest), t = t_2 and t = t_3 (back, highest). On the top slice two dots are joined by a short arrow, with the annotation 'Isometry mapping one point to another'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Homogeneity is a statement about each constant-time slice: an isometry of the slice carries any point to any other; the cosmological principle is formulated slice by slice.

redesign.idea: Slice-symmetry explorer: stacked translucent 3D slices each tiled with a pattern; the learner drags a point and sees an isometry (translation/rotation) move the whole pattern onto itself, and can switch to an inhomogeneous slice where no such map exists.
redesign.interaction: Drag point A to B; the app attempts an isometry and highlights mismatch regions if the slice is not homogeneous; a time slider scales the pattern uniformly between slices.

figures.label: Fig. 24.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Constant cosmic-time surfaces cut orthogonally by the world-lines of the substratum.
figures.visual_description: Two horizontal parallelograms labelled t = t_1 (lower) and t = t_2 (upper). Five slightly curved, diverging vertical lines (substratum geodesics, labelled at top right) pierce both, with small right-angle marks where each meets each slice. Two lines on the left are labelled x^alpha = x_1^alpha and x^alpha = x_2^alpha, showing spatial coordinates fixed along each world-line.
figures.what_it_teaches: Weyl's postulate plus isotropy: fluid world-lines are orthogonal to the slices, fan out as time increases, and carry constant comoving labels, which defines cosmic time and comoving coordinates.

redesign.idea: Comoving grid animation: a 2+1 spacetime view where galaxy world-lines fan out from a common past point, slices stack upward, and a comoving grid painted on each slice stretches with S(t) while labels stay attached to galaxies.
redesign.interaction: Scrub cosmic time; choose S(t) (linear, t^{2/3}, exponential); toggle a 'tilted' congruence to see the right-angle marks fail and a preferred direction appear.

figures.label: Fig. 24.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: What observer P maps at one cosmic time versus what P actually sees on its past light cone.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal parallelogram (labelled P's world map) through event P, which sits on the central vertical world-line among six curved diverging galaxy world-lines. Below P a cone opens downward to an elliptical base (dashed back edge); its surface is labelled on one side 'Past light cone through P' and on the other 'P's world picture'. Galaxy world-lines cross the cone at progressively earlier times the farther they are from P.
figures.what_it_teaches: Distinguishes simultaneity-based knowledge (world map) from observational knowledge (world picture): distant galaxies are seen at earlier cosmic times.

redesign.idea: Map vs picture toggle: an expanding 2+1 universe with galaxies; the learner clicks an observer event and sees two panels, the 'map' (galaxies on the current slice, at their present separations) and the 'picture' (galaxies where the past light cone intersects them, with younger colours and redshift tints).
redesign.interaction: Click observer event; slider for cosmic time; hovering a galaxy shows emission time, redshift and distance in both panels.

figures.label: Fig. 24.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The positive-curvature slice drawn as a sphere in Euclidean 4-space with one angle suppressed.
figures.visual_description: A large circle (sphere outline) with axes w (up), x (right) and z (down-left) from its centre. A horizontal ellipse near the top, dashed at the back, is labelled S^2 (chi = constant). An arc marks the angle chi from the w axis to a radius reaching the ellipse; an arc marks theta in the lower plane with a dropped perpendicular and right-angle mark. The x axis crossing of the sphere is labelled a (evidently the radius R_0).
figures.what_it_teaches: The k = +1 slice is a 3-sphere; the angle chi from a pole labels nested 2-spheres whose size grows then shrinks, giving finite volume without boundary.

redesign.idea: S^3 area meter: a globe (the 2D analogue) plus a plot panel. The learner grows a geodesic circle/sphere from a chosen point and watches measured area versus proper radius r' against the flat-space 4 pi r'^2 curve; a second mode renders S^3 by stereographic projection with nested 2-spheres.
redesign.interaction: Drag the proper radius from 0 to pi R_0; switch k = +1/0/-1 to overlay sin^2, linear and sinh^2 area laws; adjust R_0.

figures.label: Fig. 24.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Closed-model spacetime drawn as a cylinder: time along the axis, a 3-sphere as each cross-section.
figures.visual_description: Two parallel vertical lines forming a cylinder, the right line annotated 'Cosmic time t'. An ellipse across the cylinder is labelled 'Spatial slice S^3 (the epoch t = t_0)'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The topology of the k = +1 spacetime is R x S^3; the picture ignores the changing radius R(t) and shows topology only.

redesign.idea: Topology vs geometry slider: start from a straight cylinder (topology only) and morph into a 'vase' whose radius follows R(t) from a chosen Friedmann model, showing that the topology stays R x S^3 while geometry changes.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'topology' / 'geometry'; choose model parameters; scrub time to highlight a slice.

figures.label: Fig. 24.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: The negative-curvature slice drawn as a hyperboloid bowl in Minkowski 4-space with one angle suppressed.
figures.visual_description: An upward-opening bowl (one sheet of a hyperboloid) above axes w (up), x (right), z (down-left). Its lowest point is labelled R_0 on the w axis. Three horizontal ellipses (dashed at the back) at increasing heights are labelled S^2 (chi = constant).
figures.what_it_teaches: The k = -1 slice is an infinite hyperboloid; its nested 2-spheres grow without bound, faster than in flat space. The bowl looks positively curved in a Euclidean drawing, but its induced metric from the Minkowski ambient space is negatively curved.

redesign.idea: Hyperboloid in Minkowski space: a 3D bowl with a toggle between 'Euclidean ruler' and 'Minkowski ruler' measurements; geodesic triangles drawn on the surface show angle sums below 180 degrees only when the Minkowski metric is used, plus a Poincare-disc view.
redesign.interaction: Drag triangle vertices on the surface; switch ruler; read angle sum and circle circumference vs radius.

figures.label: Fig. 24.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Scale factor versus time when matter-plus-pressure dominates Lambda: a concave curve starting from zero.
figures.visual_description: Axes R(t) (vertical) and t (horizontal). A concave-down curve rises steeply from the origin and flattens to the right. A straight tangent line touches it at t_0 (vertical drop line to the axis) and extends down-left, crossing the t axis at t_1, to the left of where the curve starts.
figures.what_it_teaches: Concavity argument for the big bang: a concave expanding R(t) lies below its tangent, so it reaches zero after the tangent's intercept; the age is less than t_0 - t_1 = R/Rdot = 1/H_0.

redesign.idea: Tangent-line age bound: plot R(t) for a user-chosen mixture (matter, radiation, Lambda); draw the tangent at 'today' and shade the gap between Hubble time and true age; when Lambda dominates, the curve becomes convex and the bound visibly fails.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for Omega_m, Omega_r, Omega_Lambda and today's time; readouts H_0 t_0, q_0 and sign of rho + 3p - Lambda/4 pi.

figures.label: Fig. 24.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light ray leaving galaxy P and arriving at observer O.
figures.visual_description: A vertical line labelled O's world-line and a line tilted to the right labelled P's world-line. An arrow runs up-left from the event (t_1, r_1) on P's world-line to the event (t_0, 0) on O's world-line.
figures.what_it_teaches: Setup for integrating the radial null geodesic between emission and reception events.

redesign.idea: Conformal-time light-ray panel: show the same ray in cosmic-time coordinates (curved) and in conformal-time/comoving coordinates (straight 45-degree line), with P's comoving world-line vertical in the second panel.
redesign.interaction: Drag emission event along P's world-line; the app updates the arrival time, the integral of dt/R and f(r_1).

figures.label: Fig. 24.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two successive light signals from P reaching O.
figures.visual_description: Vertical world-line O and tilted world-line P. Two parallel arrows run up-left from P at t_1 and t_1 + dt_1 to O at t_0 and t_0 + dt (the upper label on O's line reads t_0 + dt rather than t_0 + dt_0).
figures.what_it_teaches: The spacing between successive crests is stretched on reception by R(t_0)/R(t_1), which is the origin of cosmological redshift.

redesign.idea: Wave-crest stretcher: emit a train of crests from a comoving galaxy in an expanding universe; crests travel to the observer and arrive further apart; a side plot compares received period ratio with R(t_0)/R(t_1) and with the SR Doppler formula for the 'equivalent' velocity.
redesign.interaction: Choose expansion history and source distance; step through crest emission; toggle 'SR Doppler' overlay to see the difference at high z.

figures.label: Fig. 24.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Distance measured within a constant-time slice between two galaxies.
figures.visual_description: Vertical world-line O and tilted world-line P pass through a parallelogram slice labelled t. Two dots where they cross the slice are joined by a horizontal segment labelled d_A.
figures.what_it_teaches: Absolute (proper) distance is a length taken at one cosmic time, which no observer can measure directly because light takes time.

redesign.idea: Distance zoo: one galaxy, four distances. A spacetime panel shows the emission and reception slices; bars show proper distance now, proper distance at emission, light-travel distance, and luminosity/angular distances as z increases.
redesign.interaction: Slider for redshift and cosmology parameters; bars and a log-log plot update.

figures.label: Fig. 24.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light emitted at P_1 has spread by reception time over a sphere through O_0.
figures.visual_description: Two parallelogram slices: t = t_1 (lower) and t = t_0 (upper). A vertical line (labelled r = r_0 at top; should read r = 0) passes through O_1 on the lower slice and O_0 on the upper one; a tilted line r = r_1 passes through P_1 and P_0. A cone rises from P_1 to a solid ellipse on the upper slice centred on P_0 and passing through O_0; a dashed ellipse centred on O_0 passes through P_0.
figures.what_it_teaches: Homogeneity lets one replace the sphere centred on the source with the equal-area sphere centred on the observer, whose area 4 pi R_0^2 r_1^2 is read directly off the metric.

redesign.idea: Spreading-light sphere: a 2+1 animation where a flash at P_1 expands in an expanding grid; at t_0 the wavefront sphere is outlined and its area compared with the dashed sphere centred on O; photons on the sphere are drawn redder and sparser to show the two (1+z) factors.
redesign.interaction: Scrub from emission to reception; toggle k to compare sphere area law; readout flux vs naive inverse square.

figures.label: Fig. 24.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: Sandage's 1970 compilation of redshift against corrected apparent magnitude.
figures.visual_description: Log-scaled vertical axis z with ticks 0.01, 0.1 and 1.00; horizontal axis m_corr. About sixty black data points lie along a straight diagonal band from lower left to near z ~ 0.4. Near the top the line splits into three curves labelled q_0 = 2 (bending up most steeply), q_0 = 1 (straight) and q_0 = 0 (bending toward larger magnitude).
figures.what_it_teaches: The linear Hubble law fits well over a wide range; distinguishing q_0 requires high-z data, where the 1970 data were too sparse to decide.

redesign.idea: Hubble diagram fitter: plot a historical dataset (Hubble 1929, Sandage-era, supernova-era) with model curves; the learner adjusts H_0 and q_0 (or Omega_m, Omega_Lambda) and minimizes residuals, discovering that low-z data fix H_0 while only high-z data constrain q_0.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for H_0 and q_0; dataset selector; residual plot and chi-square readout.

worked_examples.problem: Estimate the sky brightness at a point in a static, infinite, eternal, Euclidean universe uniformly filled with stars.
worked_examples.method: Divide space into concentric shells, compute each shell's contribution as luminosity over area, sum over all shells, then account for occultation.
worked_examples.key_insight: Every shell contributes the same amount, so distance does not dim the sky in aggregate; only finite age, finite extent of luminous history, or redshift can.
worked_examples.result: Naive sum \int_0^\infty \ell\,dr diverges; with blocking, sky brightness equals a stellar surface.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the scale-factor equation of a finite Newtonian universe of point galaxies with a cosmological force.
worked_examples.method: Impose spherical symmetry (radial motion), deduce uniform scaling, substitute into total energy, collect configuration-dependent sums into constants, and rescale S by mu^2 = A/|E|.
worked_examples.key_insight: Homogeneity reduces n-body dynamics to a single function S(t); energy conservation then plays the role of Friedmann's equation, with k = -sign(E).

worked_examples.problem: Show that a space isotropic about every point has constant curvature in three dimensions.
worked_examples.method: Treat G^a_b as a linear map; isotropy forbids preferred eigenvectors so G^a_b = -K delta; Bianchi identity makes K constant; trace to get R_ab = 2K g_ab/(n-2); in 3D use the Weyl-free Riemann decomposition.
worked_examples.key_insight: A symmetry argument on eigenvectors does most of the work; dimension three is special because Ricci fixes Riemann.
concepts: Riemann tensor determined by Ricci in three dimensions

worked_examples.problem: Find the spherically symmetric 3-metric of constant curvature.
worked_examples.method: Use the ansatz e^lambda dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, compute its Ricci tensor, impose R_ab = 2K h_ab and solve the resulting ODEs; then rescale r and S to reduce K to its sign.
worked_examples.key_insight: One radial function suffices, and it is fixed algebraically: e^{-lambda} = 1 - K r^2.

worked_examples.problem: Compute the area of geodesic 2-spheres and the total volume of the k = +1 slice, and interpret.
worked_examples.method: Embed via (24.41), check the induced metric, integrate the angular part for area and the full volume element over 0<=chi<=pi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Areas grow more slowly than 4 pi r'^2, peak at the equator, and shrink to zero at the antipode: a finite unbounded space.

worked_examples.problem: Embed and characterize the k = -1 slice.
worked_examples.method: Substitute r = sinh chi, embed in Minkowski space with w = R_0 cosh chi etc., verify w^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 = R_0^2, compute sphere areas.
worked_examples.key_insight: Negative curvature needs a Lorentzian ambient space; sphere areas grow like sinh^2, so volume diverges.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the Friedmann equations imply energy conservation for the cosmic fluid.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate (24.52), combine with (24.53) to eliminate Rddot, reuse (24.52), multiply by R^3.
worked_examples.key_insight: The field equations already contain the first law dE + p dV = 0, as they must by the contracted Bianchi identities.

worked_examples.problem: Prove that an expanding universe with rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi began at a finite past time, and bound its age.
worked_examples.method: Form the acceleration equation, note Rddot < 0 so the graph is concave and below every tangent; the tangent at t_0 meets R = 0 at t_0 - R_0/Rdot_0.
worked_examples.key_insight: A geometric concavity argument replaces solving any ODE; the same picture bounds the age by the Hubble time.

worked_examples.method: Set p = 0; observe that (24.53) times Rdot R^2 is a total derivative; integrate to (24.58); fix the constant using (24.52).
