worked_examples.key_insight: The integration constant C is essentially the conserved mass in a comoving sphere, and the result matches the Newtonian model term by term.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the cosmological redshift from the Robertson-Walker metric.
worked_examples.method: Integrate the radial null condition for two successive signals; since both integrals equal f(r_1), the small end intervals must match; interpret dt as proper time of comoving observers.
worked_examples.key_insight: Redshift is a ratio of scale factors, not a velocity effect: no relative velocity was ever used.

worked_examples.problem: Show redshift is proportional to distance for nearby galaxies.
worked_examples.method: Taylor expand R(t_0 - dt) to first order, and approximate the integral of dt/R by dt/R_0 and f(r_1) by r_1.
worked_examples.key_insight: Linear Hubble behaviour emerges from any smooth R(t) at small separations.

worked_examples.problem: Express the luminosity distance of a galaxy in Robertson-Walker coordinates and deduce Hubble's law.
worked_examples.method: Use homogeneity to equate the area of the wavefront sphere around the source with the sphere of radius r_1 around the observer, read area 4 pi R_0^2 r_1^2 from the metric, include (1+z)^2 dimming, compare with the definition of d_L, combine with z ~ Rdot_0 r_1.
worked_examples.key_insight: Homogeneity turns an awkward source-centred sphere into one centred on the observer; the relativistic Hubble law is then a theorem.

worked_examples.problem: Relate the deceleration parameter to density and Lambda in dust models.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate Friedmann's equation, divide appropriately to form -R Rddot/Rdot^2, then substitute C = 8 pi rho R^3/3 and H = Rdot/R.
worked_examples.key_insight: Measuring q_0 and H_0 constrains the combination of mean density and Lambda; a negative q_0 demands Lambda > 4 pi rho.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newtonian ball of galaxies with total energy E
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The relativistic scale-factor equation is shown to have the same form as energy conservation for a self-gravitating cloud: kinetic term, gravitational term, Lambda term and a constant fixed by the energy sign (k).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The meaning differs: in GR k is spatial curvature, not energy; the Newtonian model needs a centre and a finite extent, and pressure enters GR dynamics (rho + 3p) with no Newtonian counterpart.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: a Newtonian expanding ball with an energy bar chart beside an FRW model with a curvature indicator; the R(t) curves coincide for matched parameters.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: First-order equation as energy integral, second-order as equation of motion
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why (24.52) is called an energy equation and (24.53) an equation of motion, borrowing mechanics intuition.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only heuristic; both are components of one tensor equation and are related by the Bianchi identity.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Just as a gas is homogeneous only on scales containing many molecules, the universe is homogeneous only after averaging over cells over about 1e9 light years.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unlike a gas, the universe has structure on a continuous range of scales and gravitationally driven clustering; the averaging problem in GR is nontrivial (averaging then solving differs from solving then averaging).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Zoom-out slider over a galaxy distribution: density fluctuations in cells of adjustable size shrink as the cell grows.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Galaxies as particles of a fluid (substratum)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Treats galaxies like molecules carried by a smooth flow with a unique velocity at each point, justifying a perfect fluid.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real galaxies have peculiar velocities and merge; dark matter and radiation are also part of the cosmic fluid.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Extends the demotion of the Earth from the centre of the solar system to the claim that no place in the universe is special.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The Copernican idea is about our location; the cosmological principle is a strong claim about all locations and about isotropy, which requires observational support (CMB, surveys).

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Three nearby particles form a triangle; homogeneity and isotropy force it to grow into a similar triangle with a location-independent magnification, which is exactly an overall factor S^2(t) in the metric.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Local argument about small triangles; it presumes cosmic time and comoving particles already defined.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Drag triangle vertices on a comoving grid; run time forward under isotropic expansion (similar) vs anisotropic Kasner expansion (distorted).

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The area of spheres around a point in S^3 behaves like the circumference of latitude circles on a globe: nearly Euclidean near the pole, maximal at the equator, zero at the opposite pole.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: One must add a dimension mentally; the embedding space is not physical, and the analogy says nothing about time dependence.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Globe with adjustable latitude circle and live plot of circumference vs geodesic radius, then 'promote' to S^3 with areas.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Uses concavity of a curve and a straight tangent line to argue that R reaches zero within a finite past time shorter than 1/H_0.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Needs deceleration at all past times; with a positive Lambda dominating at late times the curve is convex now and the simple bound fails for today's universe.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: First law of thermodynamics dE + p dV = 0
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reads the continuity equation as an adiabatically expanding gas doing work with its pressure.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: There is no external surrounding to do work on; global energy conservation is not generally well-defined in GR, and for radiation the 'lost' energy statement is subtle.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: C as twice the mass of a Euclidean ball
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Mnemonic: the constant C = 8 pi R^3 rho/3 equals twice the mass of a sphere of radius R and density rho, linking to the 2GM/R form of an escape-speed condition.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a memory device; R is not a physical radius in the flat or open cases.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Because the closed slice has volume 2 pi^2 R^3, R is pictured as the radius of the 3-sphere.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only meaningful for k = +1; for k = 0 the normalization of R is arbitrary and for k = -1 R is a curvature radius, not a size.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian cosmology was developed first and general relativity merely refined it.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Serious dynamical cosmology began with general relativity; the Newtonian analogue was constructed afterwards and gives Friedmann's form with different interpretations of the terms.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian physics is historically older, so its cosmology is assumed older too.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An intervening absorbing gas can explain the dark night sky.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In a static eternal universe the gas heats until it re-emits as much as it absorbs, so the radiation density is not reduced.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Dust dimming works on short timescales in everyday astronomy.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Olbers' paradox disappears if space is curved or finite.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The paradox persists for non-Euclidean homogeneous space and for open or closed geometries; what matters is finite age or expansion.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Finite volume sounds like it limits the number of stars.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The universe is homogeneous in detail.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Homogeneity holds only for averages over cells larger than about 1e9 light years; below that there are galaxies, clusters and superclusters.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word 'homogeneous' is absolute in everyday language.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The cosmological principle is an established fact.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is adopted mainly because it makes the model testable with limited data; alternatives (Bianchi, hierarchical) are studied and its validity is checked observationally.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is stated like a law and underpins all standard models.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Isotropy about our location alone implies the universe is homogeneous.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Homogeneity follows from isotropy about every point; isotropy about one point is compatible with a spherically symmetric inhomogeneous universe centred on us, so the Copernican assumption is essential.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The CMB looks isotropic to us, which feels like proof of uniformity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The embedding space of the 3-sphere or hyperboloid is physically real, so the universe has an outside or a centre in the fourth dimension.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The embedding is a visual device; the slice is all of space at that epoch, with no boundary and no external points.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Diagrams show a sphere sitting in a larger space.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The sign of k fixes the global topology uniquely (k = +1 closed, otherwise infinite).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: k fixes local geometry; identifications can produce other topologies, e.g. finite flat or hyperbolic spaces.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book (and many texts) pair k with closed/open for simplicity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Einstein space' means a solution of Einstein's field equations.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In geometry an Einstein space is any metric with Ricci proportional to the metric, a purely geometric notion (though such a spacetime is a vacuum solution with Lambda).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name suggests a connection to Einstein's equations.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Cosmological redshift is the special-relativistic Doppler shift of galaxies flying through space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is set by the ratio of scale factors at emission and reception, 1+z = R_0/R_1, derived without assigning any velocity; it differs from the SR Doppler formula at large z.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: At small z both give z ~ v/c, and the book itself sometimes calls it a Doppler shift.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Luminosity distance is just the inverse-square distance from observed flux.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In an expanding universe both the photon arrival rate and each photon's energy are reduced by (1+z), and the relevant sphere area is set by R(t_0) r_1, so flux is not E/(4 pi d^2) for any single naive d.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The book's d_L is the same quantity called luminosity distance in modern cosmology papers.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Modern usage defines d_L^2 = E/(4 pi I), giving d_L = (1+z) R_0 r_1 and Hubble-law expansion z/H_0 [1 + (1-q_0)z/2]; the book's d_L divides out (1+z)^2 and equals the transverse comoving distance.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hubble's law v = H d is exact at all distances in relativistic cosmology.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The linear law holds only to first order in z (or distance); higher orders depend on q_0 and the model; very nearby it is also masked by peculiar velocities.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Taught early as a simple proportionality.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The age of the universe is always less than the Hubble time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: This holds only if the expansion has always decelerated (rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi); with the measured negative q_0 the late-time expansion accelerates and the age can approach or exceed 1/H_0 (in LambdaCDM they are nearly equal).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book's Fig. 24.8 argument is presented right before the Hubble time value.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Galaxies recede from a centre, like an explosion into pre-existing space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Uniform scaling means every galaxy sees all others receding with v proportional to distance; the Newtonian origin O is arbitrary, and comoving coordinates show galaxies at rest while the metric scales.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The Newtonian model explicitly uses an origin O and spherical symmetry about it.

thought_experiments.name: Olbers' shells
thought_experiments.setup: Surround an observer by thin concentric shells of stars in a static, infinite, eternal universe and add their light; then note every sightline eventually meets a stellar surface.
thought_experiments.lesson: Distance does not help: without finite age or expansion the sky would blaze like a stellar surface.

thought_experiments.name: Evolving triangle of particles
thought_experiments.setup: Mark a small triangle of fundamental particles at one cosmic time and look at the triangle they form later.
thought_experiments.lesson: Isotropy and homogeneity force the later triangle to be similar with a location-independent scale, so g = S^2(t)h(x).
thought_experiments.app_idea: Comoving grid with draggable triangle under isotropic vs anisotropic expansion.

thought_experiments.name: Growing spheres in a closed universe
thought_experiments.setup: From a point P at fixed epoch, measure the areas of spheres of increasing proper radius.
thought_experiments.lesson: Areas start Euclidean, fall behind 4 pi r'^2, peak at the equator, and shrink to zero at the antipode; a finite space without edge.

thought_experiments.name: Two successive light pulses
thought_experiments.setup: A comoving galaxy emits two pulses a short proper time apart; follow both to a comoving observer.
thought_experiments.lesson: The reception interval is stretched by R(t_0)/R(t_1), giving the redshift as a pure geometry effect.

thought_experiments.name: Flash spreading to a sphere through the observer
thought_experiments.setup: A galaxy flashes at t_1; by t_0 the light lies on a sphere through us; use homogeneity to find its area.
thought_experiments.lesson: The flux we receive is set by the present areal size of that sphere plus two redshift losses, which defines and computes luminosity distance.

applications_and_observations.details: In the paradoxical static model, half of the sky's radiation would come from regions so far away that light has only a 50% chance of avoiding occultation; local estimates place this beyond about 1e20 light years.
Averaging cells must exceed the largest structures (superclusters) for homogeneity to hold.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: cells over 1e9 ly; superclusters about 3e8 ly

applications_and_observations.details: Counts of quasars, radio galaxies and X-ray sources across the sky show no anisotropy above roughly the 15% level; Hubble-constant measurements from Type Ia supernovae in different directions give a comparable limit.
Thermal radiation bath discovered in 1965; Planck satellite shows isotropy to high precision; interpreted as big-bang relic.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: T = 2.7 K; isotropic to about 1 part in 100,000

applications_and_observations.details: Random motions relative to the Hubble flow are small, justifying the substratum idealization; for very nearby galaxies they obscure Hubble's law.
All forms of pressure (random stellar/galactic motions, thermal, radiation) are tiny compared with matter energy density, so dust is a good present-day model.
Quoted observational inverse Hubble constant; gives an upper bound on the age for decelerating models.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: T_0 about 1e10 yr, within a factor of 2. Modern value (our addition): H_0 about 67-73 km/s/Mpc, T_0 about 13.4-14.6 Gyr, age about 13.8 Gyr.

applications_and_observations.details: Most measurements indicate accelerating expansion; later chapter discusses details.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: q_0 = -0.6 +/- 0.3 (flat LambdaCDM with Omega_m about 0.3 gives q_0 about -0.55; our estimate)

applications_and_observations.details: Redshift against corrected apparent magnitude shows a tight linear law out to z of a few tenths; model curves for q_0 = 0, 1, 2 diverge only at the top where data are sparse. Velocity-distance law usable to about 18th magnitude.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: z from about 0.003 to about 0.5 on the plot; about 18th magnitude

applications_and_observations.details: Hubble proposed the law from eighteen nearby galaxies, a tiny corner of later diagrams.
Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae are used as sources of near-uniform luminosity, subject to calibration of absolute distances.
Some cosmologists claim understanding after the Planck-era time with GR plus GUTs; more conservatively after the electroweak era with GR plus the standard model. Big bang placed about 1e10 years ago.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (+,-,-,-): ds^2 = dt^2 - R^2(t)(...); spatial metrics d sigma^2 and h_{alpha beta} are written positive definite and enter with a minus sign.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The k = -1 embedding uses an auxiliary Minkowski metric of signature +2 (-dw^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Relativistic units G = c = 1; field equations G_ab - Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The Newtonian model keeps G explicitly.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Latin a, b, ... run 0-3 (or 1..n in general-dimension arguments); Greek alpha, beta, ... run 1-3 for spatial components.
K: actual constant curvature in R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc); k = K/|K| in {+1, -1} or 0 after rescaling.
notation_and_conventions.notes: With the book's Ricci convention a round 3-sphere has R_{alpha beta} = 2K h_{alpha beta} with K > 0.

notation_and_conventions.convention: S(t): unnormalized (Newtonian or with K); R(t) = mu S or S/|K|^{1/2}; R_0 = R(t_0).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Do not confuse the scale factor R(t) with the Ricci scalar R used in §24.7.

notation_and_conventions.convention: r (unbarred, dimensionless after rescaling), rbar (conformally flat), r* (rescaled, then starred dropped), chi (hyperspherical: r = sin chi or sinh chi), r' = R_0 chi (proper radius).
The book applies the name Robertson-Walker to the barred conformally flat form (24.37)/(24.49), but uses the unbarred form (24.36) for light propagation.
u^a with an asterisk over the equals sign: equality valid only in the particular (comoving) coordinate system.
Perfect fluid T_ab = (rho + p)u_a u_b - p g_ab with u^a u_a = +1.
z = (nu_1 - nu_0)/nu_0 with nu_1 emitted and nu_0 received; subscript 1 for emission event, 0 for observation (now).
d_A = absolute (proper) distance at fixed cosmic time; d_O = alpha/beta observational size distance; d_L = luminosity distance defined with (1+z)^2 removed.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Modern texts use d_A for angular-diameter distance and d_L without the (1+z)^2 division; beware of clashes.

notation_and_conventions.convention: H = Rdot/R, H_0 = H(t_0), T = 1/H (Hubble time, T_0 today), q = -R Rddot/Rdot^2.
Dot = d/dt with respect to cosmic time; prime = d/dr in §24.7.
ell = (number of stars per unit volume) x (mean stellar luminosity).

difficulty.notes: Mathematically lighter than the preceding black-hole and radiation chapters: the heaviest steps are the eigenvector/Einstein-space argument and the 3D Riemann decomposition, while the Friedmann equations and several transformations are left as exercises. Conceptually the challenge lies in the modelling assumptions (averaging, privileged observers, cosmic time) and the several distance definitions. The Newtonian warm-up and embedding pictures make it accessible, but notational overloading (R for scale factor and Ricci scalar; d_A and d_L conventions differing from modern usage) and some dated numbers can confuse.

teaching_gems.gem: Newtonian ball of galaxies reproduces Friedmann's equation exactly, with k emerging as minus the sign of the total energy after rescaling.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners can reach the central cosmological ODE with only first-year mechanics before touching curvature, and later recognize the relativistic result as familiar.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Energy-landscape widget: potential -C/R - Lambda R^2/3 plotted with a horizontal 'energy' line at -k; a ball rolls along R(t) and the learner sees bound (recollapse), marginal, and unbound histories.

teaching_gems.gem: Eigenvector argument: if no direction is special, the Einstein tensor viewed as a matrix must have every vector as eigenvector, so it is a multiple of the identity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts an abstract symmetry assumption into a one-line linear-algebra fact.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Show a 3x3 symmetric matrix acting on a sphere of unit vectors; generic matrices deform the sphere into an ellipsoid with principal axes (preferred directions); isotropy slider shrinks the eigenvalue differences until the ellipsoid is a sphere.

teaching_gems.gem: Similar-triangle evolution forces the metric to scale uniformly in time.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Physical, visual, and exactly captures what homogeneity plus isotropy mean for time dependence.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable triangles on an expanding grid; switching to anisotropic (Kasner) expansion distorts shapes and reveals why the cosmological principle rules it out.

teaching_gems.gem: Tracking the area of spheres versus radius distinguishes k = +1, 0, -1 intrinsically.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a measurable, embedding-free test of spatial curvature and ties directly to observations (source counts, luminosity distance).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three overlaid curves A(r') = 4 pi R_0^2 sin^2, 4 pi r'^2, 4 pi R_0^2 sinh^2 with a draggable radius; a 'galaxy count' mode shows numbers of evenly spaced galaxies inside each sphere.

teaching_gems.gem: Concave graph lies below its tangent: an expanding decelerating universe had a finite-past big bang and an age less than 1/H_0.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A theorem proved with a picture, no ODE solving; highly memorable and checkable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: See Fig. 24.8 redesign; include a failure mode when Lambda dominates.

teaching_gems.gem: Two successive light pulses give 1+z = R_0/R_1 with no reference to velocity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Cleanly separates cosmological redshift from Doppler intuition and generalizes to any wave or clock signal.
teaching_gems.app_idea: See Fig. 24.10 redesign; add a toggle comparing with SR Doppler for the same 'recession speed' to show divergence at high z.

teaching_gems.gem: Double (1+z) dimming: fewer photons per second and less energy per photon.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Physical bookkeeping that makes the luminosity-distance formula intuitive rather than a definition to memorize.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Photon-counter animation: photons arriving at a detector from a static vs expanding source, with rate and colour meters each showing a factor 1+z.

teaching_gems.gem: Use homogeneity to swap the source-centred wavefront sphere for an observer-centred one whose area is read from the metric.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A slick symmetry trick that avoids coordinates centred on the source.
teaching_gems.app_idea: See Fig. 24.12 redesign: rotate the two spheres to show they are congruent under an isometry of the slice.

teaching_gems.gem: World map versus world picture: simultaneity-based versus light-cone-based views of the universe.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Pinpoints the gap between model quantities and what we observe, preparing distance definitions and horizons.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The two Friedmann equations (24.52)-(24.53), the central result, are left entirely as an exercise without even the Christoffel symbols.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may treat the equations as given and miss how k, Rdot and Rddot arise from curvature of slices and time dependence.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide a guided derivation (Christoffels, R_00, R_ij) or a symbolic-algebra demo; point to the Newtonian analogue as a check.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed component list (24.26) is garbled: it gives R_22 = cosec^2 theta and labels the remaining expression R_33.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Someone checking Exercise 24.7 will find inconsistent results.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State R_22 = 1 + (1/2) r e^{-lambda} lambda' - e^{-lambda} and R_33 = sin^2 theta R_22.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Several small printed slips: Case 2 substitution writes x = R_0 r cos theta (should be z); maximum area said to occur at r' = pi/2 (should be r' = pi R_0/2); verbal recipe for the acceleration equation says 3 x (24.52) minus (24.53) (correct is 3 x (24.53) minus (24.52)); 'dt_1 and dt_2' should be dt_1 and dt_0; Fig. 24.12 labels O's world-line r = r_0 instead of r = 0; Exercise 24.17(i) has lower-case r(t_0) in a denominator.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers can lose time reconciling algebra with the text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Flag corrections inline in the app and in tutor answers.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book's luminosity distance divides out (1+z)^2, so d_L = r_1 R_0 and the second-order law has -(1+q_0)/2; modern literature defines d_L = (1+z) r_1 R_0 with +(1-q_0)/2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Formulas will disagree by a factor of 1+z with papers, supernova analyses and Chapter-26-style data; q_0 inferred from data could have the wrong sign convention in mind.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach both, label the book's quantity as transverse comoving (proper-motion) distance, and show how the flux relation changes.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Dated or tension-prone numbers: T_0 about 1e10 yr (factor 2), q_0 = -0.6 +/- 0.3 alongside a Sandage 1970 plot, big bang 'some 1e10 years ago', and a success of big-bang theory attributed to heavy-element abundances.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may memorize outdated values or think the big bang explains heavy elements.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Update to H_0 about 67-73 km/s/Mpc, age 13.8 Gyr, q_0 about -0.55 for LambdaCDM; clarify nucleosynthesis makes light elements (H, He, Li) while heavy elements are stellar.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Having just shown the age is below 1/H_0 when rho + 3p > Lambda/4 pi, the text quotes a negative q_0 without noting that this condition then fails today.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Creates a hidden inconsistency; learners may conclude the age bound always applies.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair (24.79) with the observation: q_0 < 0 implies Lambda > 4 pi rho now, so the tangent argument cannot be applied at t_0; in LambdaCDM H_0 t_0 is close to 0.95.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The resolution of Olbers' paradox is credited mainly to expansion redshift, and the lost photon energy is said to do the work of expansion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Modern analyses (e.g. Harrison) find finite age and finite stellar lifetimes dominate; energy-conservation claims for photons in expanding space are subtle and contested.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present both factors quantitatively (sky brightness with finite age vs with redshift) and treat the energy remark as a heuristic.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The argument that isotropy implies an Einstein space is applied in n dimensions of any signature, but for spacetime itself the cosmological principle only asserts spatial isotropy; the derivation is used only for the 3-slices, which is not clearly stated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may wrongly conclude RW spacetime is itself an Einstein space (it is not unless it is de Sitter-like).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize the argument is applied to h_{alpha beta} on each slice.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Newtonian model's origin O and finite extent are not reconciled with the claim that there is no centre; the continuum infinite case is said not to work.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may picture an explosion from a centre.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show that uniform scaling looks identical from any galaxy (change origin: velocities remain proportional to relative position).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Chapter cross-references are stale: modern cosmology, inflation and new H_0 measurements are said to be in Chapter 25 but live in Chapter 26.
Absolute distance is labelled d_A, clashing with the standard use of d_A for angular-diameter distance; the angular distance d_O is dismissed without its relativistic expression d_O = R(t_1) r_1.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Later reading will mismatch symbols; the non-monotonic angular size effect is missed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the RW angular-diameter distance and show that angular size can increase with z.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book's first-law argument (24.55) and the remark that the energy lost to redshift powers the expansion treat E = rho V as a conserved global energy, but for Lambda the same equation says vacuum energy in a comoving volume grows (p = -rho).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may generalize 'energy is conserved' to the whole universe and be puzzled once Lambda or radiation is included.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Work out dE = -p dV for dust, radiation and Lambda side by side, and stress that it is a local statement contained in T^{ab}_{;b} = 0, not a global energy budget.

tutor_notes: Open with 'Why is the night sky dark?' and let the learner reason through Olbers' shells before revealing that the answer involves the age and expansion of the universe.
Before any tensors, run the Newtonian ball-of-galaxies model: ask what the only homogeneity-preserving motion is (uniform scaling) and let the learner derive v = H r.

Check understanding of the cosmological principle by asking: 'If the CMB looks the same in all directions from Earth, what extra assumption is needed to conclude the universe is homogeneous?' (isotropy about every point / Copernican assumption).

Explain the order: principles (cosmological principle, Weyl) -> kinematics (cosmic time, comoving coordinates, S(t)) -> geometry (constant curvature, RW metric) -> dynamics (Friedmann) -> observables (z, distances, H, q). Keep a visible roadmap because the dynamics only appear two-thirds of the way through.

When introducing k, always state what it changes: local geometry of slices (area of spheres, triangle angle sums), not necessarily global topology; and in the Newtonian picture it corresponds to the sign of total energy.
Common learner question: 'Where is the centre of expansion?' Answer with the uniform-scaling argument from any galaxy's viewpoint and the comoving-grid picture.
Common learner question: 'Is redshift a Doppler shift?' Derive 1+z = R_0/R_1 from two pulses and note agreement with v/c only at small z.
Warn explicitly about the book's d_L convention (equals R_0 r_1) versus modern d_L = (1+z) R_0 r_1, and about symbol reuse of R (scale factor vs Ricci scalar) and d_A (absolute vs angular-diameter).
Quick checks: compute V = 2 pi^2 R_0^3; show that p = 0 gives rho R^3 constant; show that q_0 < 0 requires Lambda > 4 pi rho in (24.79); estimate 1/H_0 for H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc (about 14 Gyr).
For the singularity theorem, have the learner sketch R(t) with its tangent before any algebra; then ask what happens to the argument when Lambda dominates.
Update numbers when citing observations: CMB 2.725 K, H_0 about 67-73 km/s/Mpc, age 13.8 Gyr, q_0 about -0.55 in flat LambdaCDM; note the book's values are rough.
For advanced learners, connect the acceleration equation to the Raychaudhuri equation for the geodesic congruence of Weyl's postulate, and preview horizons via the integral of dt/R.
